text: In the Beginner project, Driftwood Media's Support team asked for one clean ticket report, and you built it. It's still running today. This time, a second team wants in, and what they're asking for is different enough to change the whole design, not just add a page.

Support still wants what they already have: ticket volume, category, and priority trends, kept current. Finance wants something the Beginner project's data genuinely cannot answer: how much money is going out the door in refunds, tied to those same support tickets, updated as new refunds happen. Not a one-time pull. A living number.

Here's the real gap. The Beginner project's raw dot tickets table came from a CSV export with exactly four columns: ticket ID, subscriber ID, opened-at, and category. There's no refund amount in there, no status, and no way to tell when a ticket changed after it was opened. Finance's question can't be answered with a bigger SELECT against this table, because the data it needs simply isn't in it yet.

The richer data does exist, behind the ticketing API, as JSON. Getting it into Snowflake means two real features new to this capstone: VARIANT, which lands the raw JSON payload before it's parsed, and Streams paired with Tasks, which keep the resulting model current automatically, with no person re-running anything and no watermark column to manage by hand.

One honest note before you start: this project includes a real bug on purpose. Later, after the pipeline and both Power BI pages are built, two Tasks will end up quietly consuming the same Stream, and Finance's refund total won't match what Support sees. You'll trace that down using Snowflake's own task history. Next lesson: planning the Streams-and-Tasks design before writing a single line of SQL.
